priceScope: Whole-organization annual cost per new entrant against randomized bachelor’s-degree gains and an assumed causal earnings premium; income-only welfare comparison, not a verified marginal gift offer

what: Bottom Line advises students from families under 200% of the poverty line with at least a 2.5 GPA, starting in their senior year of high school, on choosing, applying to and paying for college.
Students who enroll at one of its partner colleges keep a Bottom Line advisor for up to six years, meeting several times a semester.
This in-depth review prices the organization’s whole annual cost per new student against the extra bachelor’s degrees found in a randomized trial in Boston, Worcester and New York City.
strengths: A randomized trial of 2,422 students found 7.6 percentage points more bachelor’s degrees within five years, a 16% increase; the New York City site alone showed 7.2 points.
The gains came mainly from students enrolling at colleges with higher graduation rates and earnings, without higher net prices.
At about $4,200 per offered student in the trial, the authors find over two percentage points of added degree attainment per $1,000 spent, more than most rigorously evaluated financial-aid programs.
reservations: Our working estimate is about $1.83M per better life; all of it is income, and the earnings effect of the extra degrees has not yet been measured.
We assume a $12,000 annual earnings premium for a bachelor’s degree and treat 75% of it as causal and 80% as non-positional; these are judgments.
Average cost per new student is now about $11,985, more than double the trial’s inflation-adjusted cost, as Bottom Line expands into Ohio, Detroit and Houston and runs deficits.

sections.what: Bottom Line (The Bottom Line Inc, EIN 04-3351427) was founded in Boston in 1997 and operates in Massachusetts, New York City and Chicago, with newer sites in Ohio. Its Access program pairs high school seniors from families earning under 200% of the poverty line with full-time advisors, who meet them every three to four weeks to choose colleges, apply, complete financial aid forms and decide where to enroll. Students who enroll at one of 52 partner institutions join its Success program, with advising for up to six years. It served 6,679 students in 2023 and reports about 7,000 today across Massachusetts, New York City, Chicago, Ohio, Detroit and, from 2026, Houston. A donation supports the whole organization.
sections.monitoring: Bottom Line ran lotteries for oversubscribed places for the high school classes of 2015 and 2016, which Andrew Barr and Benjamin Castleman evaluated as a randomized trial of 2,422 students in Boston, Worcester and New York City. Degree outcomes come from the National Student Clearinghouse. The latest version is NBER working paper 33921 (2025). Arnold Ventures rates the program Top Tier and is funding a 2022–2026 follow-up on employment, earnings and debt, which has not yet reported. Bottom Line publishes annual reports with student counts. Its Chicago site opened in 2014 and was not in the trial. We have not contacted the organization.
sections.qualitative: The trial evidence on degrees is strong. Students offered advising were 7.6 percentage points more likely to earn a bachelor’s degree within five years (16% more than the control group). The first cohort showed 9.6 points within six years; an Arnold Ventures summary reports 55% versus 47% after six years. Effects were similar in the Boston area (7.4 points) and New York City (7.2 points). The authors attribute most of the gain to initial college choice: treated students were 11 points more likely to enroll where graduates earn above the median, with no significant difference in net price. Two links remain unmeasured: how much the extra degrees raise these students’ earnings, and how much of a degree’s value is positional rather than added skill.
sections.cost:
Our central estimate is **$1.83M per better life**, using ten healthy-year welfare equivalents. It is an income-only comparison: we credit no health gain. This revision replaces the first in-depth estimate of $1.10M per better life.

**Cost.** FY2025 total expense was $25.8M for about 7,000 students. Each Access senior is served for a year, and about half continue into Success advising for up to six years; at an average of 4.5 Success years, about 31% of students served are new entrants. That gives $11,985 per new student for the whole organization. The trial measured $4,161 per offered student for Access plus Success, including overhead, or about $5,534 today; the gap likely reflects start-up costs in new regions as well as inflation.

**Benefit.** Each offered student gains 0.08 bachelor’s degrees. We credit a $12,000 annual earnings premium, about a third above a $35,000 base, in line with observational bachelor’s sheepskin premiums of about 30% and with Zimmerman’s finding that marginal admission to a four-year university raised earnings 22% when only half of those admitted graduated. We count 55% of it as net household welfare after taxes, lost benefits and extra time in school, from age 23 for 35 years, discounted at 3%, on a $35,000 adult-income base. We count 75% of the premium as causal, 80% as non-positional and 85% as earned while living in the NYC metro.

**Range.** At the trial cost the estimate is $847K per better life; halfway between trial and current costs, as a mature New York site might be, it is $1.34M per better life. Using the first cohort’s six-year +9.6-point effect gives $1.53M per better life; a $6,000 premium gives $3.52M per better life; treating half the premium as positional gives $2.94M per better life. If the extra degrees do not raise earnings, there is no credited benefit.
sections.funding: Bottom Line is almost entirely funded by contributions. Revenue jumped to $36.5M in FY2023 after a $15M MacKenzie Scott grant in 2022, then fell to $23.4M and $20.2M, while expenses rose from $19.2M to $24.5M and $25.8M as it expanded into Ohio, Detroit and Houston. It ran deficits of $1.1M in FY2024 and $5.6M in FY2025, drawing net assets down from $36.6M to $27.8M. Arnold Ventures funded the trial and its earnings follow-up. A gift is likely needed to sustain current scale, but whether it adds New York students rather than funding new regions is unverified.

model.costScope: FY2025 whole-organization expense divided by new entrants derived from program structure (about 31% of students served).
model.geographicAttribution: New York City Direct students; 0.85 of adult earning years assumed lived in the NYC metro.
model.formula: Price = 10 × cost per entrant ÷ [0.5 × discounted years(35, from year 6) × ln(1 + premium × net share ÷ base) × BA effect × causal × non-positional × NYC share]. Health = 0.
model.counterfactual: Randomized control students with ordinary school counseling and any other help.
model.attribution: A gift is credited with the average effect of an added entrant at whole-organization average cost; whether a gift adds a New York student is unverified.
model.uncertainty: Dominated by the earnings premium of the extra degrees and how much is positional, then by current cost per entrant.
model.nativeOutcomes: Bachelor’s degree within five to seven years, college quality at enrollment; earnings follow-up pending.
